sections.title: Arranging a table at a neighbourhood market

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: This is the office for the market in West Court. I can reserve one table and check whether you need any additional space behind it.

script.speaker: Seller
script.text: All right. Let’s go through the details.

script.speaker: Seller
script.text: And what is the market day?

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: The market day is Saturday. On Friday the courtyard has a different event, so do not arrive with stock then.

script.speaker: Seller
script.text: Could you confirm the stall code?

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: Your stall code is B19. It is the letter B followed by one nine.

script.speaker: Seller
script.text: What have you put down for the product category?

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: I have put you in stationery. The homeware tables are at the other end of the courtyard.

script.speaker: Seller
script.text: What should I write for the arrival time?

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: Come at 7:50, or ten to eight. You can unload before visitors arrive.

script.speaker: Seller
script.text: And what is the unloading entrance?

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: Use the south entrance to unload. The northern gate is only wide enough for people on foot.

script.speaker: Seller
script.text: Could you confirm the table cover colour?

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: Bring a grey table cover. The bright banners supplied by the market will go on the back rail.

script.speaker: Seller
script.text: What have you put down for the number of chairs supplied?

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: We supply two chairs. If you need another one, tell the staff when you arrive.

script.speaker: Seller
script.text: What should I write for the waste goes into a?

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: Put waste in the bin beside the exit. The box near your stall is for spare signs, not rubbish.

script.speaker: Seller
script.text: And what is the contact person’s surname?

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: The contact surname is Lake. Ask for her at the office if anything is missing.

script.speaker: Seller
script.text: Could you confirm the vehicle leaves via the?

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: Leave with the vehicle through the alley. The path along the shops is kept clear for the public.

script.speaker: Market officer
script.text: I will send the details to you this afternoon. Keep the stall code on your phone so the volunteers can point you to the correct place.

sections.title: Finding the stations at a paper fair

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Welcome to the paper fair. All four activities lead off the central junction, and north is at the top of your plan. I will describe them before the visitors begin making their first sample.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The cutting table is north of the junction. Follow the top path to the wide, low table.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The drying rack is west of the junction, against the left wall. There are separate shelves for each group.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The display room is south of the junction, near the bottom of the plan. The doorway is next to the old notice board.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The mixing bench is east of the junction. The path on the right leads to the sink beside it.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Start by folding a narrow strip. The smaller piece is easier to handle while you practise.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Carry wet samples on a board. Holding them by one corner can tear the paper.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The demonstration paper uses blue dye. The yellow samples were prepared yesterday and are already dry.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Write your group number on the label. There will be several finished sheets with the same colour.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Put clean tools in the basket near the mixing bench. Keep the wet tools apart until they are rinsed.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The fair closes at five o’clock. Allow enough time to return the tools before then.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Finish your sample before the closing signal, then return any tools you have borrowed. Finished sheets can be collected at the entrance later.

sections.title: Planning a trial of seed containers

script.speaker: Tariq
script.text: The horticulture project compares how easy it is to remove seedlings from two types of container. We need a simple test, with observations that another team can check.

script.speaker: Lena
script.text: All right. Let’s go through the details.

script.speaker: Tariq
script.text: We are judging how easily seedlings can be removed. The colour of the containers and the total cost will be recorded separately.

script.speaker: Lena
script.text: Put the same amount of soil in each container. The containers have different shapes, and we will try two types of material.

script.speaker: Tariq
script.text: Use the first two plants for a rehearsal. We will not count them in the final data or put them on display.

script.speaker: Lena
script.text: Tariq will prepare the soil. Lena will label the pots, and Amy will check the notes after the rehearsal.

script.speaker: Tariq
script.text: Lena will label the pots on the sides. A label on the bottom would be hard to see while we work.

script.speaker: Lena
script.text: Amy will check the notes from the rehearsal. We need to know whether the scoring instructions are clear.

script.speaker: Tariq
script.text: Use the digital scale for the soil. Return the scoop to the same tray afterwards.

script.speaker: Lena
script.text: Hold each container over a tray. The tray catches loose material that would otherwise fall onto the bench.

script.speaker: Tariq
script.text: Place the seedling on a mat. That makes it easier to see soil left around the roots.

script.speaker: Lena
script.text: Put a ruler beside the plant for the last picture. It helps someone judge the scale of the image later.

script.speaker: Tariq
script.text: Write down any difficulties as soon as they happen. We can decide later which ones came from the container and which came from our method.

sections.title: Why a wall can make a garden warmer

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A wall can change both the wind and the light reaching a nearby plant. Today we will plan a comparison that records those conditions separately.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Choose a site away from the wall as your comparison. Avoid a place that is shaded by a different building.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Put both sensors at the same height above the ground. A low reading and a high reading can describe different air.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Protect the sensors from direct sunlight. We want to compare the air rather than heating the instruments.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Use a short ribbon to check the direction of the wind. It will not give a precise speed, but it shows where the air is coming from.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Write down the colour of the wall. Different surfaces can absorb or reflect different amounts of light.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Repeat the observations after sunset. The wall may continue to exchange energy with its surroundings after direct light disappears.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: If possible, place a second point on the other side of the wall. It may be exposed to a different wind.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Record whether the ground is wet or dry. The surface conditions are relevant when interpreting differences in temperature.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Use one clock for both readings. That avoids a timing difference between the two observers.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Draw a simple plan showing where the instruments stood. It is important to record distance and orientation, not just the names of the sites.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Do not describe all the effects as one temperature difference. Say where and when the readings were made and which conditions might explain them.
